title: Many EU countries have special anti-corruption agencies – but their very existence may signal systemic problems
content:
Experiences across EU countries shows that specialised anti-corruption agencies can play a crucial role in tackling political corruption, but their effectiveness depends on institutional independence and political will. While some countries have successfully prosecuted senior politicians, others continue to struggle with political interference, weakened law enforcement institutions and lengthy judicial proceedings. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office is becoming an increasingly important player in protecting EU funds and strengthening accountability.

Article:

  • Specialised anti-corruption agencies are not a solution in themselves. Their effectiveness depends on political independence, sufficient investigative powers and a functioning justice system.
  • The nine EU countries take different approaches to fighting corruption. Romania, Latvia and Lithuania have dedicated anti-corruption bodies, while Finland relies on cooperation between existing institutions.
  • Political interference remains a major obstacle. Recent institutional changes in countries such as Slovakia, Hungary, Poland and Bulgaria demonstrate how strongly anti-corruption efforts can depend on government priorities.

title: East Flank Podcast #11 The Fight Against Corruption
content:

title: Romania’s New Government: A Prime Minister in the Shadow of the PSD
content:
After nearly six months of political turmoil, Romania has had a new government since Tuesday, one dominated by the Social Democrats (PSD), who hold 12 of the 18 ministerial posts. At its head is an independent prime minister who appears to have few levers of power at his disposal.

Caught between pressure to rein in the budget deficit and the PSD’s grip on the Cabinet, new Prime Minister Luca Niculescu faces an uphill economic battle and has precious little room for political manoeuvre.

The new government takes office against a backdrop of economic hardship and deepening social polarisation. Niculescu secured parliamentary backing with the president’s threat of snap elections hanging over the vote. Yet the key portfolios remain firmly in Social Democratic hands, with one notable exception: the Finance Ministry, where Alexandru Nazare remains in post.

Aged 55, Niculescu, a former journalist and ambassador to France, faces the unenviable task of navigating two crises at once: an economy under mounting fiscal pressure and a Cabinet in which he appears to have little real authority over the PSD ministers.

title: Europe’s China visits are unlikely to deliver a trade breakthrough
content:
In October, European Commissioner for Trade Maroš Šefčovič travelled to Beijing. Following talks with Chinese officials, he announced an agreement to limit Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars to the EU. The two sides also agreed to improve access for European goods to the Chinese market and facilitate exports of rare earths and permanent magnets to Europe.

Czech politicians and business representatives are also preparing to visit China. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš (ANO) initially ruled out a trip, but announced over the summer that he could travel to Beijing in spring 2027 alongside Karel Havlíček (ANO), the minister for industry and trade. Babiš said the decision was also linked to a visit by Tomio Okamura (SPD), Speaker of the Czech Chamber of Deputies, who travelled to China in July with representatives of around 40 Czech companies.

“We have more or less agreed with Karel Havlíček that I would personally join him on an official visit next year, sometime in spring or in April,” Babiš said in July.

title: Digital euro talks gather pace as disinformation sites revive cashless society fears
content:
When the European Parliament advanced the digital euro legislation to negotiations with EU governments in July, Czech and Slovak disinformation websites began spreading claims that the new currency would spell the end of cash. The narrative is resurfacing this autumn, just as negotiations in Brussels are gathering pace.

The claims concern a real project. The European Central Bank (ECB) has been working on it for several years. Put simply, the digital euro is intended to be a banknote on your phone. The ECB describes it as a “digital form of cash”. It also sees it as a way to reduce Europe’s dependence on US card companies.

This dependence is evident in everyday card payments. More than 60% of card payments in Europe are processed through international card schemes such as Visa and Mastercard, which are owned by US companies.

Europe has no pan-European scheme of its own to compete with them, while 13 of the 21 euro area countries do not even have their own national card payment systems, ECB President Christine Lagarde has pointed out.

title: From the Black Sea to the Baltic: Drones Sink Ships and Shut Down Airports
content:
This year, drones have violated the airspace of several European countries, alarmed local populations and temporarily closed airports. In October, strikes on merchant ships off Bulgaria and Romania added a new threat to the region: attacks on sea lanes.

The attacks in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone made it the latest country to seek additional support from its allies for surveillance and protection. NATO announced it was sending more patrol aircraft, radars, drones and expert teams to the Black Sea region, while Bulgaria stepped up its air patrols.

Meanwhile, the EU is working on a common counter-drone system known as the “drone wall”, as well as a broader initiative to protect its eastern flank, including at sea.

In the space of a single week, four ships were attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. On 6 October, around 70 nautical miles east of Byala, the Alfa Watan sank and a fire broke out aboard the Able. All 18 sailors on the Able were rescued, but no survivors were found from the Alfa Watan. According to the Syrian authorities, there were ten people on board, whose fate remains unknown. The rescue operation was called off on 6 October itself.

title: AI is stealing news readers: “We can’t live on a mission alone”
content:
A journalist checks facts, interviews experts and examines documents. Producing a good news story takes hours, sometimes days. Yet readers may never make it to the publisher’s website. Instead, they see an AI-generated summary or a story selected by a social media algorithm — often with no link back to the original publication. For publishers, that means fewer visits and growing dependence on technology companies.

It is a challenge we face in our own newsroom, too. The scale of the shift is illustrated by a Pew Research Center study. Google users who were shown an AI-generated summary clicked on a conventional search result in just 8% of visits. When no AI summary appeared, that figure rose to 15%. And links embedded in the AI summaries themselves? Users clicked on those in just 1% of visits.

“If we don’t want to be manipulated, we shouldn’t leave algorithms entirely under the control of Big Tech,” Katarzyna Szymielewicz, president of the Panoptykon Foundation, tells FocusEurope.pl.

title: How Romania Is Defending the Black Sea as Russian Attacks Threaten Shipping
content:
Russian drone attacks on commercial vessels have intensified, with at least seven ships targeted in the western Black Sea, near Romania and Bulgaria, in the first half of October alone.

Reuters reported on 15 October that at least 23 seafarers had been killed or were missing following attacks on the vessels.

The attacks pose a serious threat to regional security and have prompted Romania and Bulgaria to call on NATO to strengthen its defences along the alliance’s eastern flank.

Romania’s Black Sea defences currently rely on the Romanian Naval Forces, supported by the Air Force and NATO allies, against a backdrop of mounting regional tensions.

The new Contraamiral August Roman corvette: Commissioned into service in the summer of 2026, the vessel, acquired from Turkey and belonging to the Hisar class, is currently the Romanian Navy’s most modern ship. It is now being fitted with the country’s first state-of-the-art Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship systems, recently delivered to Romania.

title: Knife Attacks in Polish Schools: What Drives Student Violence?
content:
Judging by international education assessments such as PISA, Poland appears to be a model of academic achievement. In three key areas — science, mathematics and reading comprehension — Polish 15-year-olds perform significantly above both the EU and OECD averages.

Within Europe, they are surpassed primarily by Estonia, and in certain subjects by Finland and Ireland. Yet behind these impressive results lies a deep fracture in the education system. The same research suggests that Polish students rank among the lowest in perseverance and motivation to learn. Nearly two-thirds of teenagers (63%) believe that school does little or nothing to prepare them for adult life, while 40% explicitly say that the time they spend in the classroom is wasted.
